meta.trial_name: PROVE IT-TIMI 22 (Pravastatin or Atorvastatin Evaluation and Infection Therapy-Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 22)
meta.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin); intensive LDL-C lowering with high-dose atorvastatin compared with an active comparator, standard-dose pravastatin 40 mg/day (two different statins)
meta.indication: secondary prevention of death and major cardiovascular events started within 10 days of hospitalization for an acute coronary syndrome

n_randomized.quote: We enrolled 4162 patients who had been hospitalized for an acute coronary syndrome within the preceding 10 days
n_randomized.note: Pravastatin 40 mg n=2063, atorvastatin 80 mg n=2099 (Table 1). Enrolled November 15, 2000 to December 22, 2001 at 349 sites in eight countries. 2x2 factorial with gatifloxacin vs placebo (antibiotic results not reported in S1; no interaction, P=0.90). Registry S3 lists enrollment 4000.

median_followup.note: S1 reports the mean, not the median. CTT 2010 (S5) Table 1 gives a median follow-up in survivors of 2.1 years for PROVE-IT. Eight patients (0.2 percent) were lost to follow-up.

primary_endpoint.value: Time to first of: death from any cause, myocardial infarction, documented unstable angina requiring rehospitalization, revascularization (at least 30 days after randomization), or stroke
primary_endpoint.quote: The primary end point was a composite of death from any cause, myocardial infarction, documented unstable angina requiring rehospitalization, revascularization (performed at least 30 days after randomization), and stroke.
primary_endpoint.note: Broad composite including soft components (unstable angina, revascularization). Secondary end points: CHD death, nonfatal MI or revascularization; CHD death or nonfatal MI; individual components.

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Hospitalized for ACS (MI with or without ST elevation, or high-risk unstable angina) within the preceding 10 days; stable; total cholesterol <=240 mg/dL (<=200 mg/dL if on long-term lipid-lowering therapy); not on an 80 mg statin dose
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: men and women who were at least 18 years old were eligible for inclusion if they had been hospitalized for an acute coronary syndrome
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Cholesterol limits and exclusions from the same section of S1 (read in the archived PDF). 25% were on a statin at the index event; 69% underwent PCI for the index event before randomization.

planned_events.quote: The trial continued until 925 events had been reported to the coordinating center
planned_events.note: 1001 first primary events in the final analysis (464 + 537; S2, S7).

assumed_rrr.quote: Assuming a two-year event rate of 22 percent in the atorvastatin group and that the two treatments had equivalent efficacy
assumed_rrr.note: The trial was designed to show NONINFERIORITY of pravastatin 40 mg vs atorvastatin 80 mg, not a risk reduction: 'we defined the prespecified boundary for noninferiority as an upper limit of the one-sided 95 percent confidence interval of the relative risk at two years of less than 1.17 (corresponding to a hazard ratio throughout follow-up of 1.198)' (S1). The superiority analysis was run after noninferiority was not shown. The authors' own expectation from the LDL-C difference was a 20 percent reduction (S1 Discussion).

power.quote: we determined that enrollment of 2000 patients per group would give the study a statistical power of 87 percent
power.note: Power refers to the noninferiority hypothesis, 'preserved if follow-up continued until 925 end-point events had occurred' (S1).

alpha.quote: When it was determined that noninferiority was not demonstrated, the subsequent assessment of superiority was carried out with the use of two-sided confidence intervals.
alpha.note: Two-sided 95% CI implies alpha 0.05; no alpha adjustment stated. 'Three interim assessments of efficacy and safety were carried out by the data and safety monitoring board. Rules for stopping the study early in the event that the superiority of either treatment was established were not prespecified.' (S1).

stopped_early.quote: The trial continued until 925 events had been reported to the coordinating center, after which time all patients were requested to return for a final study visit.

baseline.quote: the median LDL cholesterol levels were 106 mg per deciliter (2.74 mmol per liter) before treatment in each group
baseline.note: Measured a median of seven days after the index event (ACS lowers LDL-C acutely); 25% of patients were on a statin at baseline. Table 1 IQR 87-127 (pravastatin) and 89-128 (atorvastatin) mg/dL. CTT 2010 (S5) lists baseline LDL-C 2.62 mmol/L, footnoted as the estimated on-treatment level in the standard-statin group (no active run-in).
Table 1 medians: pravastatin 39 mg/dL (IQR 33-46), atorvastatin 38 mg/dL (IQR 32-46). Table values, not quotable as a sentence.
Table 1 medians: pravastatin 154 mg/dL (IQR 115-207), atorvastatin 158 mg/dL (IQR 119-214).
Table 1 medians: pravastatin 180 mg/dL (IQR 158-202), atorvastatin 181 mg/dL (IQR 160-205).
Not reported. Rough derivation from Table 1 medians: total cholesterol minus HDL-C = 180-39 = 141 (pravastatin), 181-38 = 143 (atorvastatin). Differences of medians are not medians of differences.

baseline.quote: Median C-reactive protein levels fell from 12.3 mg per liter at base line in each group
baseline.note: Acute-phase value measured shortly after ACS.
NOT FOUND: not reported in the main paper. ApoB/apoA-I was measured in a later substudy (S18, 2009) but baseline values were not read.
NOT FOUND: not reported in the main paper.

biomarker_effects.method: core laboratory; LDL-C reported as calculated ('calculated LDL' per S9); fasting status not captured
biomarker_effects.quote: In our study, the LDL cholesterol level was 33 mg per deciliter (0.85 mmol per liter) lower in the atorvastatin group than in the pravastatin group.
biomarker_effects.note: Active comparator, not placebo: atorvastatin 80 minus pravastatin 40. Achieved medians 62 vs 95 mg/dL (IQR 50-79 vs 79-113). change_pct derived as difference in % change from the common baseline median of 106 mg/dL: (62-95)/106 = -31.1 points; relative to the pravastatin level it is -34.7%. A difference of medians, not a mean difference. Pravastatin was blindly up-titrated to 80 mg in 8% of patients whose LDL-C exceeded 125 mg/dL.

biomarker_effects.quote: The median LDL cholesterol level achieved during treatment was 95 mg per deciliter (2.46 mmol per liter) in the standard-dose pravastatin group and 62 mg per deciliter (1.60 mmol per liter) in the high-dose atorvastatin group (P<0.001).
biomarker_effects.note: 1.60 - 2.46 = -0.86 mmol/L from the rounded abstract values; the paper states 0.85 mmol/L. The authors projected from the Heart Protection Study that this 'should translate into a 20 percent reduction in clinical events' (S1).

biomarker_effects.location: Table 1 (row text as extracted from Europe PMC XML)
biomarker_effects.note: CTT's estimate of the mean 1-year LDL-C difference (more minus less intensive arm). Smaller than the 0.85 mmol/L difference of medians in S1. Used as the calculator abs_change (same convention as tnt.json).

biomarker_effects.quote: the median LDL cholesterol levels had fallen by 22 percent at 30 days in the pravastatin group and by 51 percent in the atorvastatin group (P<0.001)
biomarker_effects.note: Among 2985 statin-naive patients (75%). In the 990 patients on a statin before entry, LDL-C was 'essentially unchanged' with pravastatin and fell 'by an additional 32 percent' with atorvastatin (S1). -29 points = -51 minus -22 (derived).

biomarker_effects.quote: Median high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels rose during follow-up by 8.1 percent in the pravastatin group and 6.5 percent in the atorvastatin group (P<0.001).

biomarker_effects.method: Biomarker core laboratory (Brigham and Women's Hospital)
biomarker_effects.quote: Median C-reactive protein levels fell from 12.3 mg per liter at base line in each group to 2.1 mg per liter in the pravastatin group and 1.3 mg per liter in the atorvastatin group (P<0.001).
biomarker_effects.note: Derived difference of medians 1.3 - 2.1 = -0.8 mg/L. Ridker 2005 (S8): reaching CRP <2 mg/L predicted outcome as strongly as reaching LDL-C <70 mg/dL, and 'meeting these targets was more important in determining the outcomes than was the specific choice of therapy'.

NOT FOUND: on-treatment triglyceride difference between arms not reported in S1. A 2008 substudy (Miller et al., JACC 2008;51:724) analysed on-treatment TG <150 mg/dL as a risk marker (abstract read; no between-arm difference given).
NOT FOUND: not reported in S1. S18 (2009) used on-treatment apoB/apoA-I as a predictor but its abstract gives no between-arm difference.
NOT FOUND: on-treatment total cholesterol and non-HDL-C by arm not reported in S1.

biomarker_effects.quote: Baseline low-density lipoprotein cholesterol level (mean, 150.2 mg/dL [3.89 mmol/L] in both treatment groups) was reduced to 110 mg/dL (2.85 mmol/L) in the pravastatin group and to 79 mg/dL (2.05 mmol/L) in the atorvastatin group (P<.001).
biomarker_effects.note: Same two regimens (atorvastatin 80 vs pravastatin 40) in an IVUS trial of 654 stable CHD patients, published 2004-03-03, five days before the PROVE IT readout. Between-arm difference 79-110 = -31 mg/dL (-0.80 mmol/L); change_pct derived as difference in % change from baseline: (79/150.2-1)-(110/150.2-1) = -47.4% - (-26.8%) = -20.6 points. CRP fell 36.4% vs 5.2% (S10).

biomarker_effects.quote: Plasma LDL cholesterol reductions from baseline were dose related, with 25% to 61% reduction from the minimum dose to the maximum dose of 80 mg atorvastatin once a day.
biomarker_effects.note: Early dose-ranging trial (1995), within-arm change from baseline, not placebo-subtracted in the abstract. Shows the expected potency of the 80 mg dose; PROVE IT observed 51% in statin-naive patients at 30 days.

hr.unit: hazard ratio (primary end point, atorvastatin 80 vs pravastatin 40)
hr.quote: Kaplan–Meier estimates of the rates of the primary end point at two years were 26.3 percent in the pravastatin group and 22.4 percent in the atorvastatin group, reflecting a 16 percent reduction in the hazard ratio in favor of atorvastatin (P=0.005; 95 percent confidence interval, 5 to 26 percent).
hr.note: The paper reports a 16% reduction (95% CI 5 to 26%), not the HR itself; HR 0.84 (0.74-0.95) is derived as 1 minus the reduction. 'The study did not meet the prespecified criterion for equivalence but did identify the superiority of the more intensive regimen' (S1). Benefit apparent at 30 days (HR reduction 17%, Fig. 3). Secondary: CHD death, MI or revascularization -14% (P=0.029); death, MI or urgent revascularization -25% (P<0.001); death from any cause -28% (P=0.07); death or MI -18% (P=0.06); unstable angina -29% (P=0.02); revascularization -14% (P=0.04); stroke not different. Baseline LDL-C >=125 mg/dL: 34% reduction vs 7% below 125 (P for interaction=0.02).

p.quote: reflecting a 16 percent reduction in the hazard ratio in favor of atorvastatin (P=0.005
p.note: Press release S2: 'There was a statistically significant difference (p=0.005) in event rates in the study over two years of follow-up'.

events_treatment.unit: patients with a first primary end point event
events_treatment.quote: At the conclusion of the study, the event rates were 537/2063 for patients randomized to pravastatin and 464/2099 for patients randomized to atorvastatin.
events_treatment.note: Atorvastatin 80 mg arm, n=2099. Confirmed by S7: 'first primary end point events were reduced by 16% with atorvastatin 80 mg versus pravastatin 40 mg (n = 464 vs. n = 537, respectively; p = 0.005)'. Event counts are not stated in the NEJM text (S1).

events_control.unit: patients with a first primary end point event
events_control.quote: At the conclusion of the study, the event rates were 537/2063 for patients randomized to pravastatin and 464/2099 for patients randomized to atorvastatin.
events_control.note: Pravastatin 40 mg arm (active comparator), n=2063. Total 1001 first events vs 925 planned.

safety_signals.value: ALT >3x upper limit of normal: 3.3% atorvastatin 80 vs 1.1% pravastatin 40 (P<0.001)
safety_signals.quote: The percentages of patients who had elevations in alanine aminotransferase levels that were more than three times the upper limit of normal were 1.1 percent in the pravastatin group and 3.3 percent in the atorvastatin group (P<0.001).
safety_signals.note: Discussion: 'there were significantly more liver-related side effects with high-dose atorvastatin than with standard-dose pravastatin', in 'a carefully selected and monitored study population' (strong CYP3A4 inhibitors excluded). The BMS release (S2) stressed this point.

safety_signals.value: Study drug stopped for myalgia or CK elevation: 3.3% atorvastatin vs 2.7% pravastatin (P=0.23); no rhabdomyolysis
safety_signals.quote: There were no cases of rhabdomyolysis in either group.
safety_signals.note: Same paragraph: discontinuation for myalgias, muscle aches or CK elevations 'in 2.7 percent of pravastatin-treated patients, as compared with 3.3 percent of atorvastatin-treated patients (P=0.23)'.

safety_signals.value: High overall discontinuation, similar in both arms: 33.0% pravastatin vs 30.4% atorvastatin at two years
safety_signals.quote: 33.0 percent and 30.4 percent, respectively, at two years (P=0.11)
safety_signals.note: At one year 21.4% vs 22.8% (P=0.30). Dose halved in 1.4% (pravastatin) vs 1.9% (atorvastatin).

safety_signals.value: No safety excess at very low achieved LDL-C (<40 or 40-60 mg/dL) on atorvastatin 80
safety_signals.quote: There were no significant differences in safety parameters, including muscle, liver, or retinal abnormalities, intracranial hemorrhage, or death, in the very low LDL groups.
safety_signals.note: Post hoc substudy of 1825 atorvastatin patients with 4-month LDL-C (2005).

genetics.finding: Genetic HMGCR (statin target) score: lower LDL-C associated with lower cardiovascular risk, nearly identical per unit LDL-C to PCSK9 variants
genetics.effect: OR 0.81 (0.72-0.90) per 10 mg/dL lower LDL-C for HMGCR
genetics.quote: odds ratio for cardiovascular events, 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 0.89) for PCSK9 and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.72 to 0.90) for HMGCR

genetics.finding: HMGCR variant rs17238484 (proxy for statin target inhibition) lowers LDL-C and modestly raises type 2 diabetes risk, mirroring statin trials
genetics.quote: Each additional rs17238484-G allele was associated with a mean 0·06 mmol/L (95% CI 0·05-0·07) lower LDL cholesterol

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization across 9 variants in 6 genes: lifelong lower LDL-C causally lowers CHD risk
genetics.effect: 54.5% (48.8-59.5%) lower CHD risk per mmol/L lower LDL-C
genetics.quote: naturally random allocation to long-term exposure to lower LDL-C was associated with a 54.5% (95% confidence interval: 48.8% to 59.5%) reduction in the risk of CHD for each mmol/l (38.7 mg/dl) lower LDL-C

genetics.finding: CTT 2010: more vs less intensive statin trials (PROVE-IT, A to Z, TNT, IDEAL, SEARCH) gave 15% fewer major vascular events for a mean 0.51 mmol/L further LDL-C reduction, proportional to the LDL-C difference
genetics.effect: 15% (11-18%) reduction for 0.51 mmol/L; RR 0.78 (0.76-0.80) per 1.0 mmol/L across all trials
genetics.quote: more intensive regimens produced a highly significant 15% (95% CI 11–18; p<0·0001) further reduction in major vascular events

consensus_explanation.summary: PROVE IT-TIMI 22, which the pravastatin sponsor designed to show that pravastatin 40 mg was noninferior to atorvastatin 80 mg after an acute coronary syndrome, instead showed that atorvastatin was superior: median on-treatment LDL-C was 62 vs 95 mg/dL, and the broad primary composite fell from 26.3% to 22.4% at two years (16% hazard reduction, 95% CI 5-26%, P=0.005; 464 vs 537 events), with benefit visible by 30 days. The investigators judged the size of the benefit 'in keeping with' the extra LDL-C lowering (they had projected about 20% from the Heart Protection Study), and the trial became a cornerstone of 'lower is better': Topol's editorial called it a 'sea change', and the CTT 2010 and Cannon 2006 meta-analyses folded it into a consistent per-mmol/L LDL-C benefit for intensive statin therapy that mainly prevents nonfatal events. Taken alone, though, the effect was modest and its upper confidence bound (0.95) was close to 1. It came mostly from unstable angina (-29%) and revascularization (-14%), while death (-28%, P=0.07) and death or MI (-18%, P=0.06) did not reach significance, and the 34% benefit was concentrated in patients with baseline LDL-C >=125 mg/dL (7% below; interaction P=0.02). The caveats the authors and reviewers raised were the comparison of two different statins (so non-lipid 'pleiotropic' effects and the larger CRP fall with atorvastatin could not be excluded; the Ridker 2005 substudy linked outcomes to achieved CRP as well as LDL-C), a short two-year follow-up, roughly 30% discontinuation, and a threefold excess of ALT elevations on 80 mg (3.3% vs 1.1%).

pre_readout.note: Key facts with a public source dated before readout_date (2004-03-08). The NEJM paper (S1), its editorial (S4) and the BMS press release (S2) all appeared on the readout day.
available_before_readout: Design: atorvastatin 80 vs pravastatin 40 mg after ACS, with a gatifloxacin factorial arm (design paper S11, Am J Cardiol 2002-04-01; abstract not available, title only read)
REVERSAL (S10, 2004-03-03): the same two regimens in stable CHD lowered LDL-C to 79 vs 110 mg/dL, cut CRP 36.4% vs 5.2%, and slowed IVUS atheroma progression (P=0.02)
Atorvastatin 80 mg lowers LDL-C by ~61% from baseline in dose-ranging data (S15, 1995)
ACC 2004 late-breaking trial listing: PROVE IT-TIMI 22 to be presented by Cannon in Session #402 on March 8, 9:45 a.m. (S17; page captured 2004-04-07, embargoed until presentation)
only_after_readout: Outcome (HR reduction, CI, P, events), achieved LDL-C and CRP, design parameters (noninferiority margin 1.17, 87% power, 925 events) and safety (S1, S2 on 2004-03-08)
Registry record (S3, first posted 2006-09-29, retrospectively registered; no results posted)
Substudies: CRP (S8, 2005), very low LDL-C safety (S9, 2005), total events 464 vs 537 first events (S7, 2009), apoB/non-HDL-C prognostic analysis (S18, 2009)
Meta-analyses: Cannon 2006 (S6), CTT 2010 (S5, 1-year LDL-C difference -0.65 mmol/L)

HMGCR genetics: Ference 2012 MR (S14), Swerdlow 2014 (S13), Ference 2016 (S12). No HMGCR-specific human genetic outcome evidence existed before readout; LDL-C causality rested on placebo-controlled statin trials.

access_summary.note: Key numbers: n, FU, planned events, assumed RRR, power, alpha, baseline LDL-C, baseline apoB, baseline Lp(a), baseline non-HDL-C, LDL-C % and abs, non-HDL-C % and abs, apoB %, Lp(a) %, HR, CI low/high, p, events x2. The 14 found in open full text are in S1, read as a 2008 Wayback Machine copy of the NEJM PDF (nejm.org itself blocks automated access); HR/CI/P and achieved LDL-C are also in the free PubMed abstract. HR and CI are derived from the reported '16 percent reduction ... 5 to 26 percent'; baseline non-HDL-C is derived from Table 1 medians; LDL-C % change is derived. Event counts (464/537) are from the BMS press release (S2) and the S7 abstract, not the NEJM text. Not found: baseline apoB, baseline Lp(a), non-HDL-C % and abs, apoB %, Lp(a) %.

sources.title: Prognostic utility of apoB/AI, total cholesterol/HDL, non-HDL cholesterol, or hs-CRP as predictors of clinical risk in patients receiving statin therapy after acute coronary syndromes: results from PROVE IT-TIMI 22
sources.note: Ray KK et al., Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol 2009;29:424-30, epub 2009-01-02. Abstract read: on-treatment apoB/AI, TC/HDL and non-HDL-C predicted events similarly to LDL-C; adding hs-CRP improved prediction. No between-arm differences in the abstract.

open_questions: The NEJM paper reports the primary result as a '16 percent reduction in the hazard ratio' with a 95% CI of 5 to 26 percent; the HR 0.84 (0.74-0.95) used here is derived from that, and the exact HR to more decimals was not found.
Primary event counts (464 vs 537) are not in the NEJM text read; they come from the BMS press release (S2) and the 2009 total-events analysis (S7), which agree.

LDL-C difference: 33 mg/dL (0.85 mmol/L) as a difference of medians during follow-up (S1) vs -0.65 mmol/L mean 1-year difference in CTT 2010 (S5). The CTT value is used for the calculator; the LDL-C % change (-31.1 points) is derived from medians relative to the common baseline median of 106 mg/dL.

Trial designed for noninferiority (pravastatin vs atorvastatin, margin RR 1.17, 87% power, 925 events); superiority was tested only after noninferiority failed, with no prespecified superiority stopping rule. assumed_rrr recorded as 0 (equivalence assumed).
Follow-up is reported as a mean of 24 months (S1); CTT gives a median of 2.1 years in survivors.

Two different statins were compared, so the trial cannot separate LDL-C lowering from statin-specific or anti-inflammatory effects (S1 Discussion; S8; S16). Later same-drug dose comparisons (TNT, SEARCH) and CTT 2010 supported an LDL-C-proportional effect.
On-treatment apoB, non-HDL-C, triglycerides and Lp(a) differences between arms were not found; LDL-C measurement described as calculated in S9 (Friedewald presumed, not stated in S1).
Topol editorial (S4) and the 2002 design paper (S11) were not read (paywalled / no abstract).

No Pfizer (atorvastatin maker) topline release was found; the readout announcement used is the sponsor's (BMS) release of 2004-03-08, readable only through the Wayback Machine (first capture 2004-03-19).
Registry S3 was registered retrospectively (2006) and lists enrollment 4000 vs 4162 randomized; registered primary outcome is 'clinical equivalence'.
The gatifloxacin factorial arm (antibiotic vs placebo) was reported separately and is not part of this case.
